question: What draws you to entrepreneurship as a field of study?
lookingFor: Genuine motivation grounded in a real experience, not just admiration of famous founders.

bullets: Ground the interest in a concrete experience, not abstract admiration
Distinguish curiosity about building things from just wanting money or fame
Connect it to what they actually want to build or solve
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I ran a small stall selling handmade candles at school fairs for two years, and what hooked me wasn't the money, it was the constant problem solving, figuring out pricing, dealing with a supplier who let me down, convincing my first ten customers to come back. I realized I loved that cycle of building something from nothing and adjusting it based on real feedback. That is what pulled me toward studying entrepreneurship properly rather than just picking it up as I go.

commonMistakes: Citing only fame or wealth as the draw
Naming a famous founder with no personal connection
Vague statements about wanting to 'make an impact' with nothing concrete
followUps: What part of that experience did you find hardest?

question: Why do you want to study entrepreneurship here specifically, rather than a general business degree?
lookingFor: Specific knowledge of program features tied to a concrete personal plan.

bullets: Name a specific program feature: incubator, seed fund, mentor network, a particular course
Explain why a dedicated entrepreneurship degree fits better than general business
Tie it to a concrete plan for what they want to build or learn
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I looked closely at your student incubator and the fact that second years can apply for the seed grant with a real pitch panel, which is rare for an undergraduate program. A general business degree would give me accounting and marketing, but I specifically want the venture-building modules where you validate an idea with real customers in the first year. I already have a rough idea around campus food waste, and this program is one of the few places where I could actually test it while still studying.

commonMistakes: Generic praise about 'great faculty' or 'good reputation'
Confusing an entrepreneurship program with an MBA
No mention of any specific resource or module
followUps: What would you do differently if you did not get into the incubator program?

question: How would you define entrepreneurship, in your own words?
lookingFor: A definition beyond 'starting a business' that captures risk, opportunity and value creation.

bullets: Go beyond 'starting a business' to opportunity recognition and value creation
Mention the role of risk and uncertainty
Distinguish it from simply running an existing, established business
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: To me entrepreneurship is spotting a gap between what people need and what currently exists, then building something to close that gap under real uncertainty, without knowing if it will work. It is different from running an established shop because you are constantly testing assumptions rather than following a proven playbook. The risk-taking matters, but so does the willingness to change the idea completely when the evidence tells you to.

commonMistakes: Defining it only as 'starting a company'
No mention of risk or uncertainty
Confusing entrepreneurship with self-employment generally
followUps: Can you think of an example of intrapreneurship, entrepreneurship inside an existing company?

question: Which matters more, the idea or the execution? Why?
lookingFor: A nuanced view that execution usually dominates, supported by a real example.

bullets: Avoid a flat either/or answer, acknowledge both matter at different stages
Argue execution is usually the bigger differentiator, with a reason or example
Show awareness that similar ideas often exist and outcomes differ on execution
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think execution matters more once an idea clears a basic bar of being useful, because most good ideas are not unique, several people are usually chasing the same gap at the same time. What separates the ones that work is how fast a team learns from customers and adjusts. I saw this with two friends who both started tutoring platforms around the same time with nearly identical ideas, and the one who actually called parents every week to ask what was not working pulled ahead within a few months.

commonMistakes: Claiming the idea alone guarantees success
Giving no example or evidence for the position taken
Refusing to actually take a side
followUps: Can a brilliant idea fail purely from bad execution? Give an example.

question: What is a minimum viable product, and why would a founder build one instead of the full product?
lookingFor: Correct definition of MVP with reasoning tied to validated learning, not just a cheap version.

bullets: Define MVP as the smallest version that tests a core assumption with real users
Explain the goal is learning, not just cutting cost
Give or reference a concrete example
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: An MVP is the smallest version of a product you can put in front of real customers to test whether your core assumption actually holds, before you spend months building features nobody wants. It is not just a cheaper product, it is specifically designed to generate feedback fast. Airbnb's founders famously started by renting out air mattresses in their own apartment to see if strangers would actually pay to stay with strangers, that tiny test told them more than a business plan ever could.

commonMistakes: Describing MVP as simply 'a low-budget version' with no learning goal
Confusing MVP with a prototype that is never shown to real users
No example to ground the explanation
followUps: What would you test first if you were building an MVP for a campus laundry app?

question: What is a book or piece of writing about entrepreneurship that has shaped how you think, and what did you take from it?
lookingFor: Genuine engagement with a specific idea from the text, not just a title drop.

bullets: Name a specific book or author, not a vague genre
Extract one concrete idea or framework from it
Connect that idea to their own thinking or a project
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I read The Lean Startup last year and the idea that stuck with me was the build-measure-learn loop, the discipline of treating every feature as a hypothesis rather than a certainty. Before that I assumed a good founder just had strong instincts about what to build. Now when I think about my own small tutoring project I try to write down what assumption I am actually testing before I add anything new, which has saved me from building things nobody asked for.

commonMistakes: Naming a book without explaining any idea from it
Picking a title that seems impressive but they clearly have not read
Only summarizing the book with no personal connection
followUps: Did you disagree with anything in that book?

question: Which entrepreneur do you admire, and what specifically about how they operate do you admire?
lookingFor: Specific, well-reasoned admiration beyond fame or net worth.

bullets: Choose someone they can speak about with real detail, not just headline facts
Focus on how the person operates or decides, not just what they achieved
Show awareness of the person's flaws or mistakes too
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I admire Sara Blakely, the founder of Spanx, mainly for how she used almost no outside funding and instead bootstrapped by cold-calling department store buyers herself with a product she had prototyped in her own apartment. What strikes me is that she treated rejection as information, she kept refining her pitch rather than assuming the product was the problem. She has also been open about early mistakes with manufacturing, which I respect because it is not the usual polished founder story.

commonMistakes: Naming a founder with no detail beyond their company's name
Idealizing the person with no acknowledgment of flaws or luck involved
Choosing someone purely because they are extremely famous
followUps: What would you ask them if you met them?

question: Your startup could grow much faster by quietly bending a regulation that is rarely enforced. What would you do?
lookingFor: Structured ethical reasoning weighing growth against integrity and long-term risk.

bullets: Acknowledge the real temptation rather than dismissing it too quickly
Reason through consequences, including trust, legal risk, and precedent for company culture
Land on a position that favors compliance or finding another path to growth
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: It would be tempting, especially early on when growth solves so many problems at once, but I would not do it. Beyond the legal risk if enforcement ever changed, the bigger cost is what it teaches the team about how we win, once bending rules becomes normal it is hard to undo. I would rather spend that energy figuring out a slower but real way to grow, and if the regulation itself seems outdated I would want to engage with it openly rather than quietly ignore it.

commonMistakes: Answering purely with 'it is illegal' and no deeper reasoning
Deciding to bend the rule because 'everyone does it'
Giving no consideration to the effect on company culture
followUps: Does your answer change if a competitor is already doing it and winning market share?

question: Pick a business idea you find interesting and explain how it would actually make money.
lookingFor: Ability to reason concretely about a revenue model, not just describe a product.

bullets: Choose a specific, describable idea rather than something vague
Identify who pays, how much, and how often
Show awareness of costs or a rough sense of margin
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I like the idea of a shared textbook rental platform for my school. Students would pay a small subscription each term instead of buying books outright, and I would also take a smaller cut from local print shops for course-pack orders routed through the platform. The subscription covers most of the fixed cost of buying and maintaining the book stock, while the print shop commission is closer to pure margin since I am not holding any inventory for that part.

commonMistakes: Describing the product in detail but never explaining the money flow
Assuming advertising alone will cover costs with no numbers behind it
Ignoring who is actually willing to pay
followUps: What would make a customer choose your platform over just buying used books directly?

question: What is the difference between bootstrapping a business and raising venture capital?
lookingFor: Clear understanding of the trade-offs, not just definitions.

bullets: Define bootstrapping as funding growth from revenue or personal savings
Define VC funding as external capital in exchange for equity, usually for speed
Note the trade-off between control and pace versus capital and growth pressure
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Bootstrapping means growing the business using its own revenue or your own savings, so you keep full control but growth is usually slower and constrained by cash flow. Venture capital means outside investors give you money in exchange for equity, which lets you grow much faster, but you give up some ownership and control, and investors usually expect a fast path to a big outcome. I think the right choice depends on whether the business actually needs speed to win, some markets punish slow movers more than others.

commonMistakes: Describing VC funding as 'free money' with no mention of equity given up
Assuming bootstrapping is always the morally superior choice
No mention of the control versus speed trade-off
followUps: What kind of business would you personally rather bootstrap than raise money for?

question: How would you know if your product actually has product-market fit?
lookingFor: Understanding of concrete signals beyond gut feeling, such as retention and organic growth.

bullets: Move beyond 'people like it' to specific measurable signals
Mention retention, repeat usage, or organic referral as evidence
Show awareness that early positive feedback can be misleading
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I would look past whether people say nice things when I ask them directly, because people are often polite, and instead look at whether they keep coming back without me pushing them to. Retention over a few weeks and whether customers refer friends without being asked feel like stronger signals than initial enthusiasm. I read that Superhuman's founder built a survey asking users how disappointed they would be if the product disappeared, and treated a high percentage of 'very disappointed' as a real signal, which I found a clever way to make the idea concrete.

commonMistakes: Relying only on early verbal praise as proof of fit
No mention of any measurable signal
Confusing a large number of sign-ups with actual product-market fit
followUps: What would you do if you tested for months and still did not find that fit?

question: Tell us about a business idea or project of yours that did not work out. What did you learn?
lookingFor: Honest account of a real setback with specific, applied learning.

bullets: Describe a genuine failure with specifics, not a disguised success
Explain what assumption turned out wrong
Show what they changed afterward, ideally with evidence
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Last year I tried selling custom phone cases online, and I spent weeks designing a website before I had sold a single case, assuming a polished storefront was what customers needed most. It turned out almost nobody found the site organically, and the two sales I did get came from a friend sharing a photo directly on Instagram. I shut the website down, learned that I should have tested demand through a simple post first, and my next small project started with a waitlist form before I built anything at all.

commonMistakes: Choosing a 'failure' that is really a humble-brag
Blaming the market or bad luck with no self-reflection
No concrete change described afterward
followUps: Would you try that idea again with what you know now?

question: Pick a problem you see often on this campus or in your city, and pitch us a business idea to solve it in under two minutes.
lookingFor: Structured on-the-spot thinking with a real problem, a plausible solution and a customer.

bullets: Name a specific, believable problem, not something invented for the answer
Propose a solution with a clear customer and rough revenue idea
Keep the pitch tight and structured rather than rambling
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Every exam season, our library runs out of group study rooms by nine in the morning, and I've watched students queue and then give up. My idea is a simple booking app just for study rooms, tied to the library's existing calendar, with a small share of slots released as short paid priority bookings during peak weeks to fund the maintenance of the system. The core booking would stay free for everyone, the paid priority option is what keeps it running without needing university budget every year.

commonMistakes: Choosing a problem too abstract to describe concretely
Skipping straight to features with no mention of who the customer is
Rambling with no clear structure or ending
followUps: What is the biggest reason this idea might not work?

question: What is the difference between an entrepreneur and someone who runs a small, established business, like a local shop owner?
lookingFor: A thoughtful distinction around growth intent and innovation, without dismissing small business owners.

bullets: Focus on intent to scale or innovate as the key distinction, not the size of the business
Avoid implying small business owners are lesser or less impressive
Note the distinction can blur in practice
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I would say the difference is less about the size of the business and more about intent, an entrepreneur is usually trying to build something new or scale an idea in a way that changes the market, while a shop owner might be running a proven model well without trying to reinvent it. That does not make the shop owner's work easier, running a local business takes huge skill and risk too. The line blurs a lot in practice, plenty of small business owners innovate constantly on how they serve customers.

commonMistakes: Implying small business owners are not 'real' entrepreneurs in a dismissive way
Basing the distinction purely on company size or revenue
Giving no nuance at all, treating it as a strict binary
followUps: Could a corner shop owner be considered an entrepreneur? Why or why not?

question: What do you understand by a 'competitive advantage' or 'moat', and why does it matter for a new business?
lookingFor: Correct concept with a concrete example of a real or hypothetical moat.

bullets: Define moat as something that protects a business from competitors copying it
Give a concrete type of moat: brand, network effect, cost advantage, patents
Explain why it matters for long-term survival, not just initial success
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A moat is whatever makes it hard for competitors to copy what you have built and steal your customers once you are successful, things like strong brand loyalty, a network effect where the product gets better as more people use it, or simply being able to produce something more cheaply than anyone else. It matters because a good idea alone gets copied fast if there is nothing protecting it, I think of WhatsApp early on, the real moat wasn't the messaging feature itself but the fact that everyone's contacts were already on it.

commonMistakes: Confusing 'moat' with simply having a good product
No specific type of moat named
Assuming a first-mover advantage alone counts as a permanent moat
followUps: What moat could a small local business realistically build?

question: How would you go about figuring out who your first real customers should be for a new idea?
lookingFor: Practical, specific approach to early customer discovery rather than vague market talk.

bullets: Suggest starting narrow with a specific, reachable group rather than 'everyone'
Mention actually talking to potential customers before building
Show awareness that the first customer segment might not be the eventual mass market
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I would start as narrow as possible rather than trying to appeal to everyone at once, probably people I can actually reach and talk to directly, like students in my own year if the idea is campus-related. I would try to have real conversations with maybe twenty of them before building anything, asking about their current workaround and what they'd be willing to pay, rather than just asking if they like the idea, because people are polite. That first narrow group might not be the eventual big market, but it's the fastest way to learn if the core problem is even real.

commonMistakes: Saying the target customer is 'everyone' or too broad to be useful
Only asking 'would you like this' instead of 'how do you solve this today'
Skipping customer conversations entirely and going straight to building
followUps: What would you do if your first ten conversations gave you mixed signals?

question: How do you think about risk when starting something new, and how much of it are you personally comfortable taking on?
lookingFor: Mature, specific understanding of risk as manageable and calculated rather than reckless.

bullets: Distinguish calculated risk from recklessness
Give a concrete personal example of a risk taken or considered
Show self-awareness about limits, not just bravado
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I don't think entrepreneurship requires being reckless, it requires being deliberate about which risks are actually worth taking and which ones you can reduce first through a small test. When I started the candle stall I was nervous about the upfront material cost, so I made ten candles first and pre-sold them to classmates before committing to a bigger batch, which cut my downside a lot. I am comfortable with risk when I can see a way to learn cheaply before betting bigger, I'm more cautious about risks where a mistake would be hard to reverse.

commonMistakes: Treating risk-taking as inherently admirable regardless of how reckless it is
Giving no personal example, only abstract statements
Claiming to have no fear or hesitation at all, which reads as unconvincing
followUps: Tell us about a risk you decided not to take. Why?

question: Why do so many successful startups have more than one founder, and what would you look for in a co-founder?
lookingFor: Understanding of complementary skills and shared decision-making, plus specific personal criteria.

bullets: Mention complementary skills as a key reason, not just moral support
Note shared workload and decision-making under pressure
Give specific, personal criteria rather than generic traits like 'trustworthy'
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A big reason is complementary skills, one person is rarely strong at building the product, selling it, and managing money all at once, so a good co-founder covers your blind spots rather than just doubling up on what you're already good at. It also helps just having someone to make hard calls with when the data is unclear, which happens constantly. For me I would look for someone whose instincts I have already seen tested under some pressure, not just someone I get along with socially, because disagreements under stress reveal a lot more than a casual friendship does.

commonMistakes: Saying 'someone I trust' with no further specificity
Ignoring the skill-complementarity angle entirely
Assuming co-founders always split equally with no discussion of roles
followUps: What would make you decide not to work with someone as a co-founder?

question: What is a value proposition, and can you write a rough one for a business idea of your choice?
lookingFor: Correct concept plus ability to apply it concretely and concisely.

bullets: Define value proposition as the specific benefit delivered to a specific customer, distinct from a tagline
Apply it to a real example with a clear customer and benefit
Keep the example concise rather than turning it into a full pitch
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A value proposition is a clear statement of the specific benefit a product gives a specific customer, and why that beats the alternatives they currently use, it is not just a catchy slogan. For an idea I've thought about, a laundry pickup service for hostel students, mine would be something like, we save time-poor students two hours a week by picking up and returning laundry on a fixed schedule, at a price close to what they'd spend on a laundromat trip anyway. It's specific about who it's for and what exactly they get.

commonMistakes: Confusing value proposition with a marketing slogan
No specific customer or benefit named
An example so vague it could apply to almost any business
followUps: How would that value proposition need to change for a different customer segment, like working professionals instead of students?

question: In your view, what is the most common reason startups fail?
lookingFor: An informed, specific answer beyond 'running out of money' with some reasoning behind it.

bullets: Go beyond the surface answer of 'running out of cash' to the underlying cause
Mention lack of real market need as a commonly cited top reason
Show awareness this can vary by industry or stage
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Running out of money is usually the immediate cause, but I think the deeper reason underneath that is usually building something people did not actually need enough to pay for, so the cash just runs out faster than revenue can replace it. Research I read from CB Insights pointed to 'no market need' as the most commonly cited reason founders themselves give when a startup shuts down. It makes sense to me, if the demand were genuinely strong, most teams would find some way to keep the lights on even with a messy business model.

commonMistakes: Stopping at 'they ran out of money' with no deeper cause
Naming a reason with no source or reasoning behind it
Treating failure reasons as identical across every industry
followUps: Does that reason apply equally to a tech startup and a small restaurant?

subtopic: Scaling and knowing when to slow down
question: Can growing too fast actually hurt a business? Explain with an example if you can.
lookingFor: Nuanced understanding that premature scaling is a real risk, ideally supported by an example.

bullets: Acknowledge growth can outpace a company's ability to deliver quality or manage cash
Give a mechanism: hiring too fast, cash burn, quality slipping, culture strain
Use a real or plausible example to ground the point
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Yes, I think growing faster than your systems can handle is one of the more overlooked risks, because everyone focuses on the fear of growing too slowly. If a company hires a large team or takes on far more customers than it can serve well, quality slips, customer trust erodes, and cash burns faster than revenue can catch up. I read that Groupon expanded into dozens of countries very quickly early on and struggled to maintain service quality and profitability in a lot of those markets, which ended up hurting the brand more than a slower, more controlled expansion might have.

commonMistakes: Assuming faster growth is always unambiguously good
Giving no mechanism for why growth causes harm
No example or evidence to support the claim
followUps: How would you personally decide when to pump the brakes on growth?

question: What skill or personal quality do you think will help you most as an entrepreneur, and what evidence do you have for it?
lookingFor: A specific, evidenced strength rather than a generic claim.

bullets: Name one specific quality, not a list of every positive trait
Back it with a concrete example or story
Show self-awareness about how that quality specifically helps in entrepreneurship
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I would say persistence in the face of small, repeated rejection. When I was trying to get local shops to stock my candles, I got told no by around fifteen shops before the first one said yes, and I kept adjusting my pitch each time based on what the previous owner said rather than getting discouraged. That kind of steady iteration under rejection feels directly useful for entrepreneurship, because most early customer or investor conversations involve more no's than yes's before something clicks.

commonMistakes: Listing several vague strengths instead of one well-evidenced one
Giving no concrete story or evidence
Naming a quality that does not clearly connect to entrepreneurship specifically
followUps: What quality do you think you still need to develop?

question: What is intrapreneurship, and is it a genuine alternative to starting your own company?
lookingFor: Correct concept plus a reasoned view on whether it substitutes for founding a venture.

bullets: Define intrapreneurship as entrepreneurial behavior inside an existing organization
Give an example, real or plausible
Offer a reasoned view on whether it can substitute for founding your own venture
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Intrapreneurship is when someone acts like an entrepreneur inside an existing company, pushing a new product or internal venture forward with real ownership, even though the company backs it financially, Gmail famously started as an internal side project at Google before it became a core product. I think it can be a genuine alternative for some people, you get real resources and less personal financial risk, but you usually have less control over the final decision and less upside if it succeeds. I'd personally want to try founding something myself first, mainly because I want the full weight of the decision-making, but I can see why intrapreneurship suits people who want the creative challenge without betting their own savings.

commonMistakes: Confusing intrapreneurship with simply having initiative at a job
No example given
Dismissing intrapreneurship entirely as 'not real' entrepreneurship without reasoning
followUps: What would make a company good at supporting intrapreneurs?

question: Take a simple business idea, say a campus coffee cart, and walk us through one strength, one weakness, one opportunity, and one threat.
lookingFor: Correct application of the SWOT framework with plausible, specific content for each quadrant.

bullets: Keep strength and weakness internal to the business, opportunity and threat external
Give specific, plausible content rather than generic filler
Show the four elements are logically connected, not random
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: For a campus coffee cart, a strength would be low overhead compared to a full cafe, since you don't need to rent a storefront. A weakness might be limited capacity during the morning rush when demand peaks hardest, since one small cart can only serve so many people at once. An opportunity is the campus currently having no coffee option within a five-minute walk of the main lecture halls, and a threat would be the university deciding to bring in its own catering vendor and squeezing out independent carts.

commonMistakes: Mixing up internal and external factors, like calling a market trend a 'weakness'
Giving generic answers like 'good product' or 'competition exists' with no specifics
The four points feel disconnected from each other rather than telling one coherent picture
followUps: Which of those four would you address first, and how?

question: Tell us about a time you spotted an opportunity, however small, and did something about it before anyone told you to.
lookingFor: Genuine initiative shown through a concrete, self-directed example.

bullets: Choose a real, specific instance of self-directed action
Show the reasoning behind spotting the opportunity, not just luck
Describe what actually happened, including any result or lesson
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: In my second year I noticed a lot of classmates buying overpriced printouts from the one shop near school before exams, so I bought a secondhand printer, negotiated a bulk paper deal, and started offering printing at a lower price out of the library during exam weeks. It was small, maybe forty rupees profit a day at first, but I noticed the gap because I was the one standing in that overpriced queue myself and got annoyed enough to actually do something about it rather than just complain. It taught me that most opportunities I've found start from being irritated by something I experience firsthand.

commonMistakes: Choosing an example that was actually assigned or suggested by someone else
Overstating the scale to sound more impressive than it was
No clear description of what action was actually taken
followUps: What stopped you from doing more with that idea?
